name: מישור במרחב
questiontext:
An affine plane in \(R^3\) is just a translation of a 2-dimensional linear subspace in \(R^3\) of the form:

\[\{w+a v + b u \ | \ a, b \in R\}\]

Where \(w,v,u \in R^3\) with \(v,u\) linearly independent. Note that usually this will not be a linear subspace but it is parallel to the linear subspace \(L=Span \{v,u\}\). The difference between any two vectors in the affine plane will be in \(L\). See for example the difference between \(v_1,v_2\) in the figure below. 

An example of a plane given by such a parameterisation is

\[P_1 : \left\{{{CT:0}} + a {{CT:1}} + b {{CT:2}} \ | \ a, b \in R^3\right\}\]

Another way in which one can describe an affine plane in \(R^3\) is as a solution of a nontrivial linear equation. 

\[\left\{{{CT:3}} \in R^3 \ | \ {{CT:3}} \cdot {{CT:4}} = C \right\} = \left\{ {{CT:3}} \in R^3 \ | \ {{CT:5}} = C \right\} \]

Again such a plane is usually not a linear plane. In fact as we know from linear algebra (and can easily check directly) the plane is linear if and only if the equation is homogeneous, i.e. \(C=0\). A concrete example for such a plane is:

\[P_2 : \left\{ {{CT:3}} \in R^3 \ | \ {{CT:3}} \cdot {{CT:6}} = {{CT:7}} \right\} = \left\{ {{CT:3}} \in R^3 \ | \ {{CT:8}} = {{CT:7}} \right\} \]

One way to understand this equation is last equation is via scalar products. If we fix \(n = {{CT:6}}\) then we are looking at the collection of all vectors in \( \{ v \in R^3 \ | \ v \cdot n = {{CT:7}}\}\). In particular this means that if \(v_1,v_2 \in P_2\) then \((v_2-v_1) \cdot n = 0\). What this means that the vector \(n\) is normal (or orthogonal) to the plane \(P_2\). 

You can see this in the figure above. The vector \(v_2-v_1\) is parallel to the plane and hence orthogonal to the normal vector \(n\). If you find it hard to imagine feel free to translate \(v_1-v_1\) so that it starts at the same point as \(n\) - as shown in the picture. Note that \(n\) is not orthogonal to the vectors \(v_1,v_2\) themselves. However one can understand the equation defining this plane also in terms of these individual vectors. Namely the plane \(P_2\) consists of all vectors \(v\) such that \(Pr_{n} (v) = \frac{v \cdot n}{n \cdot n}n = \frac{C}{||n||^2} n \}\). In other words this is the plane orthogonal to the vector \(n\) and meeting this vector on a point whose distance from the origin is \(\left| \left| \frac{C}{||n||^2} n \right| \right| = \frac{C}{||n||} \). 

It is very useful sometimes to be able to convert between these two ways of describing planes. Which is what you are asked to do below. 

Find a vector \(n_1\) and a constant \(C_1\) such that \(P_1 = \{v \in R^3 \ | \ v \cdot n_1 = C_1 \}\)

\(n_1\) = [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]],  

How to enter: each entry in its own box: a number, a fraction (e.g. 1/2) or an expression (e.g. sqrt(2)).

\(C_1\) = [[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]]

 

Now lets do the other direction. Find vectors \(w_2,v_2,u_2\) such that the plane \(P_2\) assumes the parametrization \(P_2 = \{ w_2 + a v_2 + b u_2 \ | \ a, b \in R\}\)

\(w_2 =\)   [[input:ans3]] [[validation:ans3]]

\(v_2 =\)   [[input:ans4]] [[validation:ans4]]

\(u_2 =\)   [[input:ans5]] [[validation:ans5]]

prts.name: prt1
prts.feedbackvariables: good1:if (ans1 = zervect) then false else (if crossprod(ans1,n1)=zervect then true else false);

on_true.feedback: Good. The vector \(n_1\) you entered is an orthogonal vector to the plane \(P_1\) which is what was needed here.

on_false.feedback: Sorry you got something wrong with your calculation of \(n_1\). Try choosing a non-zero vector orthogonal to the plane \(P_1\). You can find such a vector by using a cross product of the two vectors \(v = {{CT:1}}\) and the vector \(u = {{CT:2}}\) as it is given that these are linearly independent and that their directions are parallel to the plane \(P_1\). In our specific case this yields \(v \times u = {{CT:9}}\).

prts.name: prt2
prts.feedbackvariables:
good1:if (ans1 = zervect) then false else (if crossprod(ans1,n1)=zervect then true else false);
tans2:ans1.w;

on_false.feedback: The correct answer for \(C_1\) should of course be the value \(w \cdot n_1\) where \(w \in P_1\) is any vector in the plane and \(n_1\) is the normal vector that you found in the previous step. Since you didn't get the normal vector correctly it does not make sense to check the value you entered for \(C_1\). Please try again.

on_true.feedback: Yes this is a correct value for \(C_1\).

on_false.feedback: Sorry you got the wrong value for \(C_1\). You want the plane \(P_1\) to satisfy the equation \(\{v \in R^3 \ | \ v \cdot {@ans1@} = C_1\}\). So what you should do is just calculate this value for any point that is already known to be in \(P_1\). For example \(w = {{CT:0}}\), which is the vector obtained by choosing \(\alpha=\beta=0\) in the defining parametrization for \(P_1\).

on_true.feedback: Yes, the vector \(w_2 = {@ans3@}\) you chose is a good vector. Any other point contained in \(P_2\) would work just as well.

on_false.feedback: No the vector \(w_2 = {@ans3@}\) you chose is not contained in \(P_2\), which is what we need here. Any point contained in \(P_2\) would work. One such vector (i.e. a vector that solves the defining equation) in our case is \({{CT:10}}\). Another vector that you can find without solving the equation \(\frac{C}{||n||^2}n = {{CT:11}}\). Make sure you understand why this vector is contained in \(P_2\).

prts.name: prt4
prts.feedbackvariables:
cp:crossprod(ans4,ans5);
good4: if (cp = zervect) then false else (if crossprod(cp,n2)=zervect then true else false);

on_true.feedback: Yes, the two vectors that you found \(v,u\) are indeed a base to the linear space parallel to \(P_2\) which is exactly what we need here.

on_false.feedback: The vectors \(v_2,u_2\) you entered are incorrect. What you need here is a basis for the linear subspace which is parallel to \(P_2\). Such a basis can be obtained by taking the defining equation for \(P_2\) namely \(\{ {{CT:8}} = {{CT:7}}\} \) and solving the corresponding homogeneous equation \(\{ {{CT:8}} = 0\} \).
